An analyst who stopped here would have reported a compound effect as confirmed, against the field studies of @talucci2019thesis and @harvey2014, with the parent study's own machinery behind the claim. Two features of the fit argued against that reading. The product terms did not share a sign, in that grey attack raised regeneration at high severity and lowered it at low severity, and the fitted signs reversed between the two beetle surfaces on the same severity class. Adding them also moved the main effects sharply, taking the high-severity term from `r sprintf("%.3f", B_ADD[["Fire_H"]])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", B_PROD[["Fire_H"]])`, whereas a product term that was real would usually have left the rest of the model roughly where it found it.

### Spatial inference {#sec-pphonest}

Estimating the trend of a log-Gaussian Cox process by the Berman-Turner device was legitimate, because @baddeley2000 and @waagepetersen2007 showed the Poisson score to be a composite likelihood that returned consistent trend estimates whether or not the process was Poisson. The variance it reported was another matter, because the standard errors were those of the Poisson model the fit was arithmetically equivalent to, which assumed seedlings placed independently given the covariates. The estimates therefore came from the Cox specification and the uncertainty from the Poisson one, and only the second was affected.

Post-fire conifer regeneration is clustered, for reasons the field has named. @malone2018 wrote that "A clustered spatial pattern can be an indication of species having similar ecological requirements [78], facilitation among individuals [79,80], or dispersal limitations at larger scales [81]", and found regenerating conifers "clustered at distances up to at least 30 m", and @ziegler2017 found that "All species had aggregated spatial patterns, with aggregation greatest at smaller scales" and that their Cox models "underpredicted tree densities at smaller distances". The parent study itself established the same for this pattern, in that it tested the observed pattern against 999 Monte Carlo simulations of Ripley's inhomogeneous K under a null of non-constant intensity and reported significant clustering for every species examined [@murphy2026]. The residuals of the refit said the same thing directly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlogram
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Residual dependence at the two scales the study worked at. Left, the conditioned severity model of @sec-severity across the burn, where dependence had largely decayed by 500 m. Right, the fit with product terms over the quadrature points inside the regeneration plots, where it had decayed by about 100 m. Each panel set the block sizes tried at its own scale."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 3.2

pres <- function(X, b) {
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% b)) * PP$w
  (PP$yy * PP$w - mu) / sqrt(mu)
}
rq <- pres(X_PROD, B_PROD)[!PP$data_pt]
rq <- rq - mean(rq)
set.seed(7)
jj <- sample(nrow(Q), min(2500L, nrow(Q)))
dd <- as.vector(dist(cbind(Q$x[jj], Q$y[jj])))
rr <- outer(rq[jj], rq[jj]) / mean(rq[jj]^2)
rr <- rr[lower.tri(rr)]
pbins <- cut(dd, c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, Inf))
PCORR <- tibble(`Lag (m)` = levels(pbins),
                `Residual correlation` = round(as.numeric(tapply(rr, pbins, mean)), 3)) |>
  filter(!is.na(`Residual correlation`))
invisible(keep(PCORR, "fig-correlogram"))

## Bin midpoints for plotting. cut() labels are "(a,b]", and the open final bin
## has no midpoint, so it is dropped rather than given an invented one.
mid_of <- function(lab) {
  n <- regmatches(lab, gregexpr("-?[0-9.]+|Inf", lab))
  vapply(n, function(v) mean(as.numeric(v)), numeric(1))
}
corr_df <- function(x, scale) {
  x |> mutate(Lag = mid_of(`Lag (m)`), Scale = scale) |>
    filter(is.finite(Lag)) |> select(Lag, r = `Residual correlation`, Scale)
}
CORR_BOTH <- bind_rows(
  corr_df(CORR,  "Across the burn, severity model"),
  corr_df(PCORR, "Inside the plots, fit with product terms"))

FIG_CORR <- ggplot(CORR_BOTH, aes(Lag, r)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "22", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, colour = "#7b3294") +
  geom_point(size = 1.9, colour = "#7b3294") +
  facet_wrap(~ Scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Lag (m)", y = "Residual correlation") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8))
CORR_PATH <- file.path("..", "03.outputs", "PNG", "fig-correlogram.png")
ggsave(CORR_PATH, FIG_CORR, width = 7.2, height = 3.2, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
knitr::include_graphics(CORR_PATH)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppcorr
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Residual correlogram of the fit with product terms over the quadrature points inside the plots, the right panel of @fig-correlogram at the precision that set the block sizes tried."

show(PCORR, "tbl-ppcorr", "lr")
```

Residual dependence inside the plots ran at `r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[1]` within 25 m and was still `r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[3]` between 50 and 75 m, crossing zero at around 100 m (@tbl-ppcorr, @fig-correlogram right). A block that contained it therefore had to be at least 75 to 100 m on a side, and a 200 m plot gave few of those, the same conflict @sec-blocks met at landscape scale, two orders of magnitude smaller.

```{r}
#| label: fig-interaction
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The four product terms and the main effects they modified, under the Poisson likelihood the published model was fitted with and under a spatial block bootstrap across block sizes spanning the residual range. The estimate was the same in every case and only the interval changed. Product terms that excluded zero under the Poisson likelihood excluded it at no block size."
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4.4

pp_boot <- function(X, side_m, seed = 11) {
  ids <- split(seq_len(nrow(PP)), paste(PP$x %/% side_m, PP$y %/% side_m))
  K <- length(ids)
  set.seed(seed)
  M <- vapply(seq_len(B_BOOT),
              function(b) pfit(X, unlist(ids[sample.int(K, K, TRUE)], use.names = FALSE)),
              numeric(ncol(X)))
  ci <- apply(M, 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Term = colnames(X), Lower = ci[1, ], Upper = ci[2, ], K = K,
         Usable = apply(M, 1, function(v) sum(is.finite(v))))
}

PP_SHOWN <- c("MPB_G", "MPB_R", "Fire_H", "Fire_L", PRODT)
PPB_RAW <- bind_rows(lapply(PP_SWEEP, function(m)
  pp_boot(X_PROD, m) |> filter(Term %in% PP_SHOWN) |> mutate(`Block side (m)` = m)))

## The ground each product term is estimated from, quadrature points where both
## of its indicators are on. This is what a resample has to miss for the term to
## become unidentified, so it is the number that explains the Usable counts.
PROD_CELLS <- vapply(PRODT, function(t) {
  v <- strsplit(t, ":", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  sum(Q[[v[1]]] == 1 & Q[[v[2]]] == 1)
}, integer(1))

## Identification, carried forward rather than averaged away. A term is fully
## identified at a block size only if every one of the B_BOOT draws estimated it;
## anything less means some resample omitted the blocks carrying its cells, and
## the percentile for that term is then taken over a selected subset of draws.
PPB_RAW <- PPB_RAW |> mutate(Identified = Usable == B_BOOT)

PPB <- PPB_RAW |>
  transmute(`Block side (m)`, Blocks = K, Term,
            Estimate = round(B_PROD[Term], 3),
            Interval = ci_txt(Lower, Upper),
            `Draws` = paste0(Usable, "/", B_BOOT),
            ` ` = ifelse(clears(Lower, Upper), "clears zero", "spans zero"))
invisible(keep(PPB, "fig-interaction"))

## The published likelihood's own interval, drawn beside the block intervals so
## the comparison the paper rests on is one figure rather than two tables.
## Design-matrix column names are not axis labels. Written once here and reused
## by the verdict chunk below, so the figure and the prose cannot disagree.
PP_WORDS <- c(MPB_G = "grey attack", MPB_R = "red attack",
              Fire_H = "high severity", Fire_L = "low severity")
pp_label <- function(term) {
  parts <- strsplit(term, ":", fixed = TRUE)
  vapply(parts, function(v) {
    lab <- paste(PP_WORDS[v], collapse = " by ")
    paste0(toupper(substring(lab, 1, 1)), substring(lab, 2))
  }, character(1))
}

SRC <- c("Poisson likelihood", paste(PP_SWEEP, "m blocks"))
PPF <- bind_rows(
  tibble(Term = PP_SHOWN, Lower = B_PROD[PP_SHOWN] - 1.96 * SE_PROD[PP_SHOWN],
         Upper = B_PROD[PP_SHOWN] + 1.96 * SE_PROD[PP_SHOWN], Source = SRC[1]),
  PPB_RAW |> transmute(Term, Lower, Upper,
                       Source = paste(`Block side (m)`, "m blocks"))) |>
  mutate(Estimate = B_PROD[Term],
         Source = factor(Source, levels = SRC),
         Kind = factor(ifelse(grepl(":", Term), "Product terms", "Main effects"),
                       levels = c("Main effects", "Product terms")),
         Term = factor(pp_label(Term), levels = rev(pp_label(PP_SHOWN))))

FIG_INT <- ggplot(PPF, aes(Estimate, Term, colour = Source)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "22", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = Lower, xmax = Upper),
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), size = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b2182b", "#c6dbef", "#6baed6", "#2171b5", "#08306b"),
                      name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(Kind ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1, reverse = FALSE)) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8, angle = -90))
INT_PATH <- file.path("..", "03.outputs", "PNG", "fig-interaction.png")
ggsave(INT_PATH, FIG_INT, width = 7.4, height = 4.4, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
knitr::include_graphics(INT_PATH)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppblocks
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The same intervals as numbers, with the count of bootstrap draws that identified each term. A term short of the full count was unestimable in some resample because the blocks carrying its cells were not drawn, and its interval is then a percentile over the draws that did identify it."

show(PPB, "tbl-ppblocks", "rrlrlrl") |> collapse_rows(1:2, valign = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sandwich
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "A second variance estimate, independent of the bootstrap. Standard errors for the fit with product terms under the naive Poisson likelihood and under a cluster-robust sandwich clustered on the same spatial blocks, with the ratio between them."

## A block bootstrap over 14 to 36 blocks sits below the percentile method's
## comfortable floor, so the inference should not rest on it alone. The sandwich
## is the check a referee will already trust. The bread is the same Poisson
## information pois_ci inverts, and the meat is the outer product of scores
## summed within block, so dependence inside a block is carried and dependence
## between blocks is assumed away. Same assumption as the bootstrap, different
## estimator.
cluster_se <- function(X, b, side_m) {
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% b))
  V  <- solve(crossprod(X, X * (mu * PP$w)))          # bread: Poisson information
  U  <- (PP$w * (PP$yy - mu)) * X                     # score contribution per point
  S  <- rowsum(U, paste(PP$x %/% side_m, PP$y %/% side_m))
  G  <- nrow(S)
  ## The usual finite-cluster correction. With G this small it is not cosmetic.
  meat <- crossprod(S) * (G / (G - 1))
  sqrt(diag(V %*% meat %*% V))
}

SAND <- bind_rows(lapply(PP_OK, function(m) {
  se <- cluster_se(X_PROD, B_PROD, m)
  tibble(`Block side (m)` = m, Term = PP_SHOWN,
         `Poisson SE` = round(unname(SE_PROD[PP_SHOWN]), 3),
         `Cluster-robust SE` = round(unname(se[PP_SHOWN]), 3),
         Ratio = round(unname(se[PP_SHOWN] / SE_PROD[PP_SHOWN]), 1),
         lo = B_PROD[PP_SHOWN] - 1.96 * se[PP_SHOWN],
         hi = B_PROD[PP_SHOWN] + 1.96 * se[PP_SHOWN])
}))

## The same verdict the bootstrap was asked for, from the other estimator.
SAND_PROD_CLEAR <- sum(clears(SAND$lo[SAND$Term %in% PRODT],
                              SAND$hi[SAND$Term %in% PRODT]))
SAND_N_PROD <- sum(SAND$Term %in% PRODT)
SAND_RANGE  <- range(SAND$Ratio)

show(SAND |> select(-lo, -hi) |>
       mutate(Term = pp_label(Term)), "tbl-sandwich", "rlrrr") |>
  collapse_rows(1, valign = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: pp-verdict
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Let the sweep state the conclusion. Asserting one that a refit could
## invalidate is the error sec-blocks records having made once already.
PROD_ROWS  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(Term %in% PRODT)
PROD_CLEAR <- sum(clears(PROD_ROWS$Lower, PROD_ROWS$Upper))

MAIN_KEEP  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(!Term %in% PRODT) |>
  group_by(Term) |> summarise(all_clear = all(clears(Lower, Upper)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(all_clear) |> pull(Term)
MAIN_WORDS <- paste(tolower(pp_label(MAIN_KEEP)), collapse = " and ")

## PP_OK, the block sizes the correlogram licenses, is declared in setup because
## tbl-sandwich needs it upstream of here.
PP_OK_K  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(`Block side (m)` %in% PP_OK) |>
  distinct(`Block side (m)`, K) |> arrange(desc(K))
PP_OK_TXT <- paste(sprintf("%d at %d m", PP_OK_K$K, PP_OK_K$`Block side (m)`),
                   collapse = " and ")
## The widening factor is the paper's headline number, so it is computed only
## where every draw identified the term. A partially identified term has an
## interval taken over a selected subset of resamples, which inflates it for a
## reason that has nothing to do with spatial dependence, and quoting that as
## the cost of honest inference would overstate the case.
DEGEN <- PPB_RAW |> filter(!Identified)
WIDEN <- PPB_RAW |> filter(Identified) |>
  mutate(naive = 2 * 1.96 * SE_PROD[Term], ratio = (Upper - Lower) / naive) |>
  summarise(lo = min(ratio), hi = max(ratio), n = n())

## The abstract lives in the YAML, where an inline `r` expression does not run, so
## its seven quantities are the only hard-coded numbers in the document. They are
## asserted here instead, so a refit that moves any of them fails the render rather
## than leaving the abstract quietly contradicting the results.
## This guard is only real with `error: false` in the YAML. Under `error: true`
## a failure here printed nothing at all, because the chunk also sets
## `output: false`, and the render exited 0 with the abstract contradicting the
## results. That is how the previous 2.4 and 7.6 survived a refit that moved
## them. Do not set `error: true`, and do not remove `output: false` in place of
## fixing it, because the chunk's console noise is not the point of it.
if (B_BOOT == 2000L) stopifnot(
          sprintf("%.3f", SEV_ADJ) == "0.043",
          N_CLEAR == 0,
          LR_P < 0.001,
          sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo) == "2.3",
          sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi) == "5.9",
          nrow(PROD_ROWS) == 16,
          PROD_CLEAR == 0,
          SAND_PROD_CLEAR == 0)
```

None of the `r nrow(PROD_ROWS)` product-term intervals excluded zero across the four block sizes (@fig-interaction, @tbl-ppblocks). The estimates did not move, because the estimates were not what the Poisson likelihood got wrong, and the intervals widened by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)` against the naive Poisson intervals of @tbl-ppproduct, which was the whole of the difference between a compound effect that looked overwhelming and one that was absent. The cluster-robust sandwich agreed on both counts (@tbl-sandwich), inflating the standard errors by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", SAND_RANGE[1])` to `r sprintf("%.1f", SAND_RANGE[2])`, in the same range as the bootstrap widening, and of the `r SAND_N_PROD` product-term intervals it implied across the block sizes the correlogram supported, `r SAND_PROD_CLEAR` excluded zero. The two estimators shared the assumption that blocks were independent of one another and differed in everything else, in that the bootstrap resampled blocks and the sandwich summed scores within them.

The widening factor was computed only over the `r WIDEN$n` of `r nrow(PPB_RAW)` term-by-block combinations that every one of the `r format(B_BOOT, big.mark = ",")` draws could estimate. The four product cells rested on `r min(PROD_CELLS)` to `r max(PROD_CELLS)` quadrature points each, so a resample that missed the blocks holding one of them left that term unidentified, and `r nrow(DEGEN)` combinations were affected, every one involving red attack or high severity, the worst losing `r B_BOOT - min(PPB_RAW$Usable)` draws of `r format(B_BOOT, big.mark = ",")`. The percentile for such a term was taken over whichever resamples happened to contain its cells, which were the resamples that overweighted them, and that inflated the interval for a reason unconnected with spatial dependence; left in, those combinations put the top of the widening range at `r sprintf("%.1f", max((PPB_RAW$Upper - PPB_RAW$Lower) / (2 * 1.96 * SE_PROD[PPB_RAW$Term])))` rather than `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`. The count of usable draws is reported in @tbl-ppblocks for every cell, and none of it changed the verdict, because the affected intervals were already the widest and every product term spanned zero on the identified combinations alone.

The only terms among those shown whose intervals excluded zero at every block size were `r MAIN_WORDS`, neither of them a product term, so the regeneration data supported main effects for red-stage beetle attack and low burn severity and supported no statement about the two causes acting together. Three plots totalling `r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha gave `r PP_OK_TXT` across the block sizes the residual range permitted, and a product term asked those blocks to resolve a difference of differences across four severity-by-attack combinations. The published likelihood answered the question confidently because it counted `r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` seedlings as `r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` independent pieces of evidence.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Principal findings {#sec-found}

In the Darkwoods Conservation Area, prior beetle attack did not change the probability that a cell burned at high severity in 2015. The log-odds for attacked against unattacked cells were `r sprintf("%.3f", SEV_ADJ)` (block bootstrap interval `r ci_of(M_ADJ, "y")`) with lodgepole presence and elevation in the model, the interval spanned zero at every block size tried, and the count of attack years showed no hump-shaped effect. Lodgepole presence had the largest coefficient, `r sprintf("%.3f", gv(M_ADJ, "host"))` (`r ci_of(M_ADJ, "host")`), with cells holding the host less likely to burn at high severity.

The compound effect was not supported. Under the likelihood the parent study used it was decisive [χ^2^(`r LR_DF`) = `r sprintf("%.1f", LR_STAT)`, `r if (LR_P < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else sprintf("p = %.3f", LR_P)`], with `r N_PROD_SIG` of `r LR_DF` product terms excluding zero. Under inference that accounted for the clustering of the seedling pattern every product term spanned zero at every block size tried, and a cluster-robust sandwich clustered on the same blocks agreed. The estimates did not move and the intervals widened by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`, which was the whole distance between a confirmed compound effect and none.

## Linked disturbance {#sec-linked}

The null on the linked effect agreed with the field studies of this forest type. @talucci2019thesis found "minimal or no effects of outbreak severity on fire severity" across the subalpine literature and "six of seven fire effects showing no evidence of an effect" in her own plots, @harvey2014 found the effect small beside weather, and @liang2016 found severity "unrelated to pre-fire outbreak severity" across an ecoregion. The one form this study could not test was hers, the hump in the probability of high severity at intermediate outbreak severity after accounting for fire weather, because a single fire gave no weather contrast and, as she put it, "In subalpine forests, fuels become relatively less important as a controlling variable when fire weather becomes extreme (Bessie and Johnson 1995), while under moderate fire weather conditions, fuels may be more important for burn severity." The attack-year count stood in for her continuous outbreak severity and showed no curvature, but the count ran from zero to `r length(YR_LIVE)` over a window that closed four years before the fire, and whether the Mt Midgeley fire burned under moderate or extreme weather is not recorded in these surfaces.

The moderate class carried a measurement caveat that any severity-class analysis inherits. @lentile2006 reported that high-severity fire produced more homogeneous effects than moderate or low, so at 30 m the moderate class is the most mixed, and @talucci2019thesis noted "discrepancies between field observations and satellite-measured change" where prefire mortality existed. Modelling high severity against the rest, as she did, kept the least mixed class as the response, which is one reason the reversed form of the first objective was preferred to a tabulation of attack across classes.

## Compound disturbance {#sec-compound}

The null on the compound effect likewise agreed with the field. @talucci2019thesis found recruitment driven by fire severity and cone abundance "while substantial underlying tree mortality from the MPB outbreaks did not play a role", and that "Sub-boreal lodgepole pine forests are generally resilient when MPB outbreaks and wildfire recur in short intervals", and @harvey2014 found no direct effect of outbreak severity on initial lodgepole regeneration. @liang2016 reported a positive compound effect on seedling reestablishment from an area ratio and qualified it themselves against Harvey. The parent study's abstract sentence about overlapping mortality and high severity was a statement of the feedback @krawchuk2020 described, in which beetle-killed canopy reduces the seed source a fire refugium supplies, and this study found that the data the parent study built could not support that feedback either way, which meant the additive specification was the right one to have fitted. The finding was therefore not a revision of the parent study's ecology but a statement about what these data could be asked, with the limit located in the inference rather than in the landscape.

The mechanism of the disagreement between the Poisson fit and the field studies was not specific to this landscape. A point process trend fitted by the Berman-Turner device was a weighted Poisson regression [@berman1992; @baddeley2000], and a Poisson likelihood counted every seedling as an independent piece of evidence about the covariates, whereas post-fire regeneration clusters through dispersal limitation, facilitation and shared microsite [@ziegler2017; @malone2018]. The parent study devoted two figures and 999 Monte Carlo simulations to establishing that the seedling pattern was clustered [@murphy2026], and the residual correlogram of @fig-correlogram reached the same verdict from inside the model with dependence of `r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[1]` within 25 m. How the intervals of covariate effects in inhomogeneous point process models of regeneration should be computed once that clustering is admitted is a question the point-pattern literature has not settled, in that @ziegler2017 relied on replication across eighteen plots and a random effect for fire, @malone2018 reported least-squares fits without stating the error model, and the parent study reported Poisson errors. The block bootstrap and cluster-robust sandwich used here are two answers among several, and the size of the correction they returned, a widening of `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`, is what this study can contribute to that question.

The caution this implied was not new. Modelling conifer regeneration after a large mixed-severity fire, @donato2009 excluded from their candidate set any model with more than five predictors or any interaction term, on the stated ground that the sample was too modest to support them, and reported relative importance among additive predictors instead. That was a judgement made in advance, on a study of comparable design and larger extent, and it reached by prior reasoning the conclusion this paper reached by measurement, which put a number on the room the data in fact allowed.

## Extent constraints {#sec-extent}

Every result here was bounded by an extent chosen by a disturbance rather than by a design. The burn covered about eight square kilometres and the regeneration plots totalled `r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha inside it, which was the ground on which beetle and fire co-occurred at all, so not an arbitrary choice, but not a neutral one either. Across the burn, lodgepole cover and elevation correlated at r = `r sprintf("%.2f", R_PL_EL)` and could not be separated, where the companion study distinguished them because 1,776 m of relief held pine-poor ground at every height [@murphy2026refugia]. The same conflict governed the inference at both scales, because a block bootstrap needed blocks large enough to contain the dependence and numerous enough to resample, and the extent capped the first before the second was comfortable, with `r SWEEP$Blocks[SWEEP$"Block side (m)" == BLOCK_M]` blocks of 500 m across the burn where 1 km would have given eight, and `r PP_OK_TXT` inside the plots where the residual range demanded 75 to 100 m.

Both results were nulls, and a null has a floor set by its sample. Nothing here showed that beetle mortality and burn severity did not interact; it showed that `r format(N_FR, big.mark = ",")` cells in `r K_500` blocks could not detect a linked effect of the size these surfaces could record, and that `r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` seedlings across `r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha, clustered as this pattern was, could not resolve a difference of differences across four severity-by-attack combinations. Residual dependence that neither the bootstrap nor the sandwich captured would have left every interval still too narrow, which for two null results was a conservative failure, because a fuller accounting could only widen intervals that already spanned zero.

The first objective was answered inside the perimeter only, because the comparison the linked-disturbance literature makes, between attacked stands that burned and attacked stands that did not, needed beetle surfaces that reached beyond the burn, and recovering it would mean rebuilding the classification over the unclipped landscape. The severity reference category of the regeneration model was inherited rather than chosen, because the published specification had indicators for high and low severity only and pooled moderate severity with unburned and unclassified ground into a reference that was `r round(100 * REF_MOD / REF_N)` per cent moderate; it was reproduced rather than repaired, because the object was to test the published model rather than replace it. The provincial survey was a coarse instrument, its polygons sketched from an aircraft at a mapping scale far coarser than 30 m, and it was used only to test whether ground outside the perimeter was attacked at all, which it could answer, and not to measure severity, which it could not.

## Research priorities {#sec-next}

Of the three tasks that follow, in descending order of value against cost, the first is to repeat the compound-effect test where extent is not the binding constraint, which given the dependence range measured here means a distributed plot network rather than three contiguous plots. The published point process results should be reported with intervals that respect the clustering, which is inexpensive because the estimates are unchanged and which on the evidence of @fig-interaction leaves two main effects standing. Testing the linked effect in the form of @talucci2019thesis, with fire weather as a covariate, requires more than one fire or a fire whose weather record spans the burn, and rebuilding the beetle classification over the unclipped landscape would restore the comparison across the perimeter that these surfaces could not make.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

This study tested, on the data of the parent study, the two effects the field distinguishes between a beetle outbreak and the fire that follows it, and found neither, in agreement with the field studies of lodgepole pine at short intervals. Prior attack did not change the probability of high-severity burning within the Mt Midgeley burn, at `r sprintf("%.3f", SEV_ADJ)` in log-odds after conditioning on host and elevation with an interval spanning zero at every block size the extent supported, and the count of attack years showed no hump. The beetle by fire product terms were decisive under the published Poisson likelihood and absent under inference that accounted for the clustering the parent study itself documented, with identical coefficients either way and intervals that differed by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`.

The additive model of the parent study was therefore the defensible one, because nothing found here supported modelling beetle and fire any other way with data of this extent, and the apparent support for doing so came from a likelihood that counted clustered seedlings as independent observations. A compound effect of beetle and fire on regeneration in this landscape has not been demonstrated, these data could not demonstrate it, and the size of the correction that separated a confident interaction from none was the finding that applies elsewhere.
